title: Security Deposits in India: How to Get Yours Back
description: What the law actually says about rental security deposits in India, why landlords withhold them, and the move-in protocol that gets yours returned in full.
excerpt: It's the biggest cheque most renters write, and the least documented. Here's what the law says, why deposits go missing, and the boring paperwork that gets yours back.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: Renters, landlords, and people who've lost a deposit

hero.alt: A set of house keys resting on a signed rental agreement beside a moving box in an empty apartment

faq.q: How many months of rent can a landlord legally take as a security deposit in India?
faq.a: It depends on your state. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 recommends a cap of two months' rent for residential premises and six months' for non-residential ones. But it is a model law — a template the central government circulated for states to adopt. Unless your state has enacted its own tenancy law with that cap, the amount is whatever your agreement says. Check your state's status before assuming a cap protects you.

faq.q: Why are most rental agreements in India exactly 11 months?
faq.a: Because of the Registration Act, 1908. A lease of immovable property from year to year, or for a term exceeding one year, must be registered. An 11-month agreement falls below that threshold, so landlords avoid registration and its stamp duty. It is a workaround, not a legal requirement, and an unregistered agreement is weaker evidence if you ever need to prove your terms.

faq.q: Can a landlord deduct for normal wear and tear?
faq.a: Generally no, and this is the single most common dispute. Faded paint, minor scuff marks and ageing fittings are the cost of a property being lived in. Actual damage — a cracked basin, a burnt countertop, a missing geyser — is different. The problem is almost never the principle; it is that nobody documented the condition on day one, so it becomes your word against theirs.

faq.q: What should I do if my landlord refuses to return the deposit?
faq.a: Start with a written request by email or letter, itemising the amount and the date you vacated, and keep a copy. If that fails, send a formal legal notice through a lawyer. Where a state tenancy law is in force, there is usually a Rent Authority or Rent Court to approach; otherwise the route is a civil suit or consumer forum. The realistic lesson is that recovery is slow and expensive, which is exactly why the documentation you do at move-in matters more than any remedy afterwards.

faq.q: Should I pay the security deposit in cash?
faq.a: Avoid it. Pay by bank transfer, UPI or cheque so the payment has a trail with a date, an amount and a named recipient. A cash deposit with only a handwritten receipt — or no receipt — is the weakest position you can be in, because the first thing disputed is often whether you paid what you say you paid.

faq.q: Does a registered rental agreement protect my deposit?
faq.a: It does not guarantee a refund, but it makes your terms provable rather than arguable. A registered agreement is admissible evidence of what both sides agreed, including the deposit amount and refund timeline. Some states, such as Tamil Nadu, require tenancy agreements to be registered with a rent authority. Registration is a cost worth weighing against the size of the deposit at stake.

body:
Ravi moved out of his Bengaluru flat on a Saturday. He'd lived there three years, never missed a rent payment, and left the place cleaner than he found it. His landlord shook his hand, said the deposit would be transferred "in a week or ten days," and that was the last straightforward conversation they had.

The first week passed. Then a message: there were some repairs. Then a list — repainting, a chipped kitchen tile, a door that didn't close properly. By the time the money arrived, seven weeks later, ₹1.4 lakh had become ₹62,000.

Ravi had no photographs of the flat on the day he moved in. No inventory. No written note of the door that had never closed properly from the start. He had a WhatsApp thread, a rental agreement that said "deposit refundable on vacating," and a strong sense of injustice — which, it turns out, is not evidence.

You've probably heard a version of this story. You may have lived it.

Here's the uncomfortable part: in most of these cases the landlord isn't a villain. They're working from memory too, and memory conveniently favours whoever is holding the money.

## The biggest cheque nobody documents

Think about the sums involved. In much of urban India a security deposit runs anywhere from two months' rent to ten, depending on the city and how the local market has always done things. For a flat at ₹35,000 a month, a six-month deposit is ₹2.1 lakh handed to someone you met three weeks ago.

It is, for most renters, the largest single payment they make that year. Larger than the deposit on a car. Comparable to a wedding.

And it is routinely handed over with less paperwork than opening a bank account.

No condition report. No photographs. No itemised list of what's in the flat and what state it's in. Often no clear written statement of *when* the money comes back or *what* can be deducted from it. Just a line in an agreement saying the deposit is refundable, which sounds reassuring right up to the moment it needs to mean something specific.

That gap — between how much money is at stake and how little is written down — is where almost every deposit dispute in India lives.

## Why this keeps happening

It would be easy to blame landlords. It's also mostly wrong, and it stops you from fixing anything. Four structural things make deposit disputes the default rather than the exception.

### There is no single national tenancy law in force

This surprises people. Rental housing in India is a state subject, and for decades most states ran on old rent control legislation written for a different economy.

In June 2021, the Union Cabinet approved the **Model Tenancy Act, 2021**. It is a genuinely sensible document. It proposes a cap on security deposits — a maximum of two months' rent for residential premises, six months' for non-residential. It requires the landlord to refund the deposit at the time the tenant vacates. It sets up a Rent Authority, a Rent Court and a Rent Tribunal so disputes don't have to go through ordinary civil courts. It even requires a landlord to give notice before entering.

Here's the catch, and it's the single most misreported fact about renting in India: **a model law is a template, not a law**. The central government circulated it for states to adopt, adapt or ignore. Until your state enacts its own tenancy legislation, the two-month cap protects you exactly as much as a good idea in a PDF.

So when someone tells you confidently that "the law now says two months," the honest answer is: it depends entirely on which state you're standing in. Check your own state's status. Do not assume.

### The 11-month agreement is a workaround, and it weakens you

Ever wondered why virtually every rental agreement you've signed runs for exactly eleven months?

It's not a coincidence and it's not a convention. Under the **Registration Act, 1908**, a lease of immovable property from year to year, or for any term exceeding one year, must be registered. Registration costs money, takes time, and creates a public record.

Eleven months sits just under the threshold. There is more to that document than its length — [what every clause is doing](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india) is worth reading before you sign one. So the whole country writes eleven-month agreements, renews them, and writes them again.

The consequence is quiet but real: an unregistered agreement is weaker evidence. If you ever have to prove what was agreed about your deposit, you're relying on a document that was deliberately structured to avoid official record. That's not fatal. But it's not the strong position most people assume they're in.

Some states have moved on this. Tamil Nadu, for example, requires tenancy agreements to be registered with a rent authority through a state portal. That is a meaningfully better arrangement for both sides — worth knowing whether your state has something similar.

### "Normal wear and tear" is undefined until it's disputed

Nearly every agreement says the landlord may deduct for damage but not for normal wear and tear. Nearly none define where the line sits.

Is three years of sunlight fading a wall normal wear? Most people would say yes. Is a repaint therefore the landlord's cost? Most landlords would say no.

Both positions are arguable, which is precisely the problem. The dispute isn't usually about principle. It's about the fact that neither party recorded what the wall looked like when you got the keys.

### The money sits with the person who decides

This is the structural asymmetry underneath everything else. Your landlord holds the deposit and also decides what to deduct from it. You can disagree, but disagreement doesn't move money.

And the remedy is genuinely disproportionate. Pursuing ₹40,000 through a civil suit can cost more than ₹40,000 in fees and years in time — which is the honest shape of [most tenant remedies in India](/blog/tenant-rights-in-india). Most renters do the arithmetic, feel sick about it, and let it go.

Which means the leverage you have is almost entirely front-loaded. Everything that protects your deposit happens before you move in — not after you move out.

## The move-in protocol that actually works

None of this is clever. It's boring, it takes about ninety minutes, and it is the difference between getting ₹2 lakh back and arguing about it for two months.

### 1. Photograph everything, on the day you get the keys

Before a single box comes in. Empty rooms, good light.

Walls and ceilings in every room. Floors, especially near doorways and windows. The inside of every cupboard. Bathroom fittings, taps, the flush, the geyser. The kitchen counter, sink, and the back of the platform. Window grilles, latches, mosquito mesh. Switchboards. Any furniture or appliance the landlord is providing.

Then photograph every single defect you can find, close up. The stain, the chip, the door that sticks, the tap that drips. You are not being difficult. You are recording a baseline.

Critically: **your phone timestamps these**. That metadata is doing real work. Take them on the day, not a fortnight later.

### 2. Take a video walkthrough and narrate it

A slow two-minute walk through the flat, speaking as you go. "Second bedroom, this is the crack near the window, it's already there on the eighth of August."

A narrated video is remarkably hard to argue with, and it takes less time than reading this paragraph.

### 3. Write an inventory and condition report — and get it signed

One page. Two columns: item, condition. Every appliance and fitting the landlord is providing, with its state and any existing damage noted plainly.

Both of you sign it. Both of you keep a copy. Attach it to the agreement.

Most landlords will agree to this without a blink, because it protects them too — it's their evidence that the geyser was working when you arrived. If a landlord refuses to sign a factual record of the flat's condition, you have learned something important about how the end of this tenancy is going to go.

### 4. Make the agreement say something specific

"Refundable on vacating" is not a term. It's a sentiment. Push for language that answers actual questions:

- **How much** is the deposit, in figures and words
- **When** it is returned — a number of days from handover of keys, not "promptly"
- **What** may be deducted, and the requirement that deductions be itemised in writing with proof of cost
- **That normal wear and tear is excluded**, stated explicitly
- **Whether repainting is chargeable**, because this is the most common single deduction and it should not be a surprise
- **What happens to unpaid utility bills** at the end

You will not get everything. Asking for it changes the conversation anyway, because it signals you'll be keeping records.

### 5. Pay so the payment is provable

Bank transfer, UPI, or cheque. Never cash if you can avoid it.

A traceable payment has a date, an amount and a named recipient, and it cannot be re-remembered later. Get a receipt as well — but the bank record is the thing that matters.

> If you take one thing from this article: photograph the empty flat on day one and pay the deposit through a bank. Those two habits cost you an hour and resolve most disputes before they start.

### 6. Do the same walkthrough on the way out

Same rooms, same angles, after your things are gone and the place is cleaned. Ideally with the landlord present.

Then hand over the keys with a short written note — an email is fine — confirming the date you vacated, the meter readings, and that you're requesting the deposit back per the agreement. That email starts a clock, and it exists.

## Common mistakes, in rough order of how much they cost

**Paying before seeing the agreement.** Token advances get requested early — one of [several payments that never appear in the advertised rent](/blog/hidden-costs-of-renting-in-india), often to "hold" a flat. Once your money is with someone, your negotiating position on every remaining term is worse.

**Accepting a verbal promise about the refund timeline.** "A week or ten days" is not a term. It's a mood.

**Not photographing, because it feels awkward.** Ninety minutes of mild social discomfort against a six-figure sum. Everyone who has lost a deposit says the same thing afterwards.

**Assuming a law protects you that isn't in force where you live.** See above. Verify your own state.

**Letting rent adjust against the deposit at the end.** Landlords sometimes suggest you skip the last two months' rent instead of a refund. It sounds efficient. It also destroys your leverage — you've now used part of the deposit, the balance is fuzzy, and if there's a dispute about damage you've already spent your bargaining chip. Keep rent and deposit as separate transactions.

**Leaving without written confirmation of the handover date.** Without it, the timeline can be re-remembered.

**Not reading the maintenance clause.** Many agreements make the tenant responsible for repairs under a certain value. That's often reasonable. It's less reasonable when you discover it at move-out.

## A few things experience teaches

**Ask the previous tenant.** It is the single highest-value question in the whole process, and there are [others worth having ready](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting). If you can meet them, or even reach them, ask one question: did you get your deposit back, and how long did it take? No inspection tells you as much about a landlord as the answer.

**Meet the actual owner at least once.** If every conversation runs through a caretaker or a relative, find out who legally owns the property and whose account the deposit is going into. Deposits get complicated when it's unclear who is holding them.

**Be a slightly annoying tenant about written records, and a genuinely easy one about everything else.** Report problems in writing and fix small things without drama. The paper trail protects you; being reasonable is what makes a landlord want to refund you promptly.

**Get repairs acknowledged in writing while you live there.** If the landlord agrees a leak is a structural issue and their responsibility, you want that in a message thread, not just in a phone call. It will be a different conversation in eighteen months.

**Treat the deposit as spent money until it lands.** Don't plan the next flat's deposit around getting this one back on time. Renters get squeezed badly by that assumption every month.

**Negotiate the deposit, not just the rent.** In many markets there's more flexibility on deposit than on monthly rent, especially with owners who've had a flat empty for a while. It's asked for far less often than it should be.

## Where this fits into how we built StayOnMap

We'll be honest about the limits here, because a rental platform promising to solve deposit disputes would be overselling. We don't hold your deposit, and we can't make a landlord refund it.

What we can do is remove the information gaps that make the whole arrangement lopsided.

Every listing on StayOnMap states the deposit as a required field, alongside the rent, maintenance, and any other charges — so the number is visible before you visit, not sprung on you in a hallway. There's no brokerage, which removes the other large opaque payment renters make. And because you're speaking to the owner directly rather than through an intermediary, the person answering your questions about the deposit is the person who will be returning it.

We also show you the neighbourhood around a home on the map — what's genuinely near it, how far things actually are — because the other expensive rental mistake is signing for a place that turns out to be forty minutes from everything you need.

That's the honest scope: better information, fewer intermediaries, and the terms written down where you can read them.

## What to remember

A security deposit is the largest cheque most renters write and the one they document least. That imbalance, not landlord villainy, is what causes most disputes.

The law is uneven. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 proposes real protections — including a two-month cap for homes — but it only binds you where your state has enacted it. Find out where yours stands rather than assuming.

And almost all of your leverage exists before you move in. The photographs, the signed condition report, the specific refund clause, the traceable payment — that's ninety minutes of work that decides how the last week of your tenancy goes.

Ravi rents somewhere else now. First thing he did with the keys, before the boxes came up, was walk through the empty flat with his phone out, talking to himself about a scratch on the bedroom door.

He got that deposit back in eleven days.
